column5: Once a client's present and desired states are named, NLP offers a specific toolkit for closing the gap.
column7: The guide says naming both states comes before the toolkit for closing the gap; the workbook gives the reader a written way to describe both states and choose a first change.

column5: An idea is loose and untested, while a goal, done properly, has already survived some contact with reality before it is written, and the Present State to Desired State Model gives the gap its clearest shape.
column7: The sentence says this model gives the gap its clearest shape; the workbook lets the reader work the model on one area of their own life.

column5: The gap between your present state and your desired state isn't empty space but the ground on which the real adjustment is made.
column7: The page treats the gap as ground where adjustment is made; the workbook adds seven steps for describing each state truthfully and choosing the first change.

column5: No two people see anything in quite the same way, which means no single perspective is automatically right or automatically wrong, and two accounts of one event can differ sharply while both stay true to what each person saw.
column7: The page says two accounts of one event can differ and both be true; the workbook shows the route from event through filters to response and has the reader test one reaction.

column5: By the end of this guide you'll be able to say where some of your own limiting beliefs came from and to see how a belief filters what you notice.
column7: The guide promises the reader will see how a belief filters what they notice; the workbook names the filters and the generalising, distorting and deleting they do to an event.

column5: The section starts with how you read an ordinary moment, moves on to the models your mind uses to reach a conclusion and the biases and distortions that steer that conclusion off course, and ends with tools for changing how you think.
column7: The guide opens with how a person reads an ordinary moment; the workbook teaches the model of how an event becomes a reading and has the reader separate the event from the story.

column5: Most writing on the subject stops at the inner half, with advice to name your emotions and notice your triggers.
column7: The guide argues emotional intelligence needs a social half; the workbook sets out the four areas in order and has the reader mark each against a real week.

column5: Achology teaches self-awareness as the foundation of all four, with self-discipline and social awareness built on top of it.
column7: The guide places self-awareness under social awareness and self-discipline; the workbook shows why each of the four areas rests on the one before and lets the reader choose which to grow.

column5: In his 1995 book *Emotional Intelligence: Why It Can Matter More Than IQ*, the psychologist Daniel Goleman gave the loose idea of "people skills" a structure, built from self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skill.
column7: The page gives Goleman's structure of self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy and social skill; the workbook gives the four-area sequence and an exercise on the reader's own week.

column5: We tend to assume that maturity arrives along with the birthdays.
column7: The page says maturity does not come with birthdays; the workbook gives a seven-level ladder to place one hard situation on.

column5: Age doesn't define maturity, whatever most of us assume, and what defines it is a willingness to take full responsibility for your actions, choices, consequences and ongoing growth.
column7: The guide says maturity is taking full responsibility; the workbook shows the levels of that responsibility from victim to free creation and names the next level's ask.

column5: Karpman's model names one role Victim, and it describes a way of seeing a situation that anyone can fall into, where the situation seems insurmountable, something happening to a person and not something they can act on.
column7: The sentence describes the Victim position; the workbook puts Victim at the bottom of a seven-level ladder and shows what climbing from it asks.

column5: A fixed outlook also argues hard for its own labels.
column7: The page says a fixed outlook defends its labels as fact; the workbook has the reader find where one label started and write a truer definition.

column5: Achology's own view is that a mindset is something you are in and not something you have for life, so nobody is a fixed type, and most of us are open in one part of life and closed in another.
column7: The page says nobody is a fixed type and mindset varies by area; the workbook helps the reader test one label they live inside.

column5: The course opens on a distinction that most of us never draw aloud, the difference between a fixed mindset and a growth mindset.
column7: The guide opens on the fixed and growth contrast; the workbook teaches it through labels and unlearning, with a written exercise on one label.

column5: The stance is simple to state, since the person is the one expert on her own life and a helper's contribution is therefore questions that open things up and attention that stays on her.
column7: The page says the person is the expert on her own life; the workbook has the reader name who they have handed a decision to and take it back.

column5: Then ask yourself: where in your own week has someone in authority asked you to go along, and what did you really believe about it at the time?
column7: The page ends by asking where someone in authority asked the reader to go along; the workbook separates advice to learn from instructions to obey.

column5: Freedom, then, is something you build through responsibility and not something that circumstances hand you, and in Achology's view that is good news, since a life that is yours to own is yours to change.
column7: The page says a life that is yours to own is yours to change; the workbook shows whose rules the reader lives by and how to take advice yet still decide.

column5: The first is to wait, so that when someone finishes speaking you pause for two breaths before you answer and see what happens to the conversation.
column7: The page advises pausing when someone finishes speaking; the workbook adds the four habits of a flexible mind and a test of one firm view through each.

column5: Psychological flexibility is the ability to adapt your thinking as circumstances change, and rigidity is its opposite.
column7: The guide defines flexibility as adapting your thinking; the workbook teaches understanding an idea before judging it, with four habits to practise.

column5: Three practical habits help us prepare, and the first is staying open-minded and flexible, because flexibility is the key to stability and not its opposite.
column7: The page names staying open-minded and flexible as the first habit; the workbook sets out the habits of a flexible mind and has the reader apply them to one view.

column5: Chunking up means zooming out towards a more abstract level of thought, and in practice it usually comes down to one question: for what purpose?
column7: The page explains moving to a more abstract level with one question; the workbook teaches concrete and abstract thinking and has the reader take one open question up and down the ladder.

column5: Another idea in the same teaching dates from 1931, when the mathematician Alfred Korzybski proposed that the map is not the territory.
column7: The page introduces Korzybski's point that the map is not the territory; the workbook builds on his idea of abstracting and what an answer shows about the reader's map.

column5: Chunking up moves a conversation towards a bigger, more general idea, and chunking down moves it towards a smaller and more specific one that you can almost touch.
column7: The guide describes moving between general and specific; the workbook shows how to tell a checkable question from an open one and stay with the open one.

column5: NLP runs on nine basic presuppositions, which are working assumptions and not proven facts, and Achology teaches them as a set from the first part of the course.
column7: The guide names the nine presuppositions as working assumptions; the workbook lets the reader try them as attitudes on one difficult person.

column5: Skilled helping rests on a set of presuppositions, much as [life coaching](/learn/helping-people/articles/life-coaching/) does.
column7: The guide says helping rests on presuppositions; the workbook gives the reader the nine NLP ones to test on a real relationship.

column5: Coaches also work from presuppositions, assumptions they adopt because working from them produces better conversations, even though none can be proved.
column7: The page says coaches adopt unprovable assumptions because they improve conversations; the workbook sets out NLP's nine and practises three.

column5: An identity grounded in virtues such as honesty, integrity, kindness, patience, creativity, and fairness will remain sustainable because virtues simply do not change.
column7: The page says virtue-based identity is sustainable; the workbook has the reader list how they define themselves and rewrite it around virtues.

column5: A sharp line separates personality from the true self.
column7: The page draws the line between personality and the true self; the workbook explains the difference and applies it to the reader's own self-definition.

column5: An identity anchored in a role, a past result or a group's expectations can cap what a person becomes, whereas one anchored in what they stand for always has room to grow.
column7: The page warns that identity tied to a role or past result caps growth; the workbook shows the six places people look and the virtues alternative.

column5: We all carry a set of perceived limits, the things we believe we can do and the things we believe we can't, and the word to notice is perceived.
column7: The page treats limits as perceived and testable; the workbook takes eight questions through one area of life to sort real limits from self-set ones.

column5: The obstacle is rarely a lack of ability, and far more often it's a rigid way of thinking about what ability is and where it comes from.
column7: The page says the obstacle is rigid thinking; the workbook teaches mental flexibility as a habit and gives questions to loosen it.

column5: Outgrowing your limiting beliefs rarely happens in one clean moment, because a belief sits inside a whole structure of habits and expectations, and that structure gives way a piece at a time.
column7: The page says limits give way a piece at a time; the workbook makes revisiting limits a repeated habit with a question set to return to.

column5: The other is to connect, which treats a disagreement as an invitation to compare maps.
column7: The page invites comparing maps in a disagreement; the workbook has the reader draw both sides of one disagreement and find the question each missed.

column5: Another idea in the same teaching dates from 1931, when the mathematician Alfred Korzybski proposed that the map is not the territory.
column7: The page introduces Korzybski's map and territory in passing; the workbook teaches the idea in full and applies it to a real argument.

column5: Achology's teaching on perception says the same thing in other words: the map is not the territory, and your view of the world is a map drawn from snapshots, never complete.
column7: The page ties opinions mistaken for facts to the map not being the territory; the workbook works the idea through one disagreement.

column5: The wise mind is an idea that comes from DBT, and we teach it as a way to understand how you handle your thoughts and make decisions.
column7: The page introduces the rational, emotional and wise minds; the workbook has the reader hear one real decision from each before choosing.

column5: The wise mind model separates the reasoning mind, the emotional mind and the wise mind, the place in between where the other two meet.
column7: The page uses the wise mind model to check a mood; the workbook teaches the model in full and practises it on a decision.

column5: A rational mind is driven by logic and fact, an emotional mind is driven by feeling, and a wise mind balances the two and does not favour either alone.
column7: The guide states the three minds in one line; the workbook shows balance as a pendulum and walks through one decision.

column5: The Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP) tradition has a precise name for what happens when you assume, which is your frame of reference.
column7: The page names the frame of reference as what assumptions run on; the workbook traces where the reader's sense of normal was formed.

column5: Your frame of reference is the standpoint you use to understand and evaluate things, and it supplies context and something to compare against.
column7: The page defines the frame of reference in one line; the workbook has the reader trace one everyday habit back to where they learned it.

column5: A frame of reference is difficult to see from inside because it doesn't announce itself, so your sentence keeps passing as fact.
column7: The page says the frame is hard to see from inside; the workbook gives a way to see it by tracing and testing one habit.

column5: The course builds on this with a model of three separate parts of state, all resting on old and simple advice: know yourself.
column7: The page names three parts of state through the wasp story; the workbook has the reader sort one of their own strong reactions among them.

column5: In short, transference is the other person's old material turning up in you.
column7: The page explains old feelings landing on someone in front of you; the workbook has the reader judge whether a feeling is inside, present or from the past.

column5: In Achology's view a feeling is a state you're in and not a fixed part of you, and a state can be understood and moved through.
column7: The page treats a feeling as a state that can be understood; the workbook shows the three places a state can come from and what each allows.

column5: Anchoring links a feeling to a cue, such as a gesture or a word, so that the cue brings the feeling back.
column7: The page names anchoring among NLP techniques in one line; the workbook explains the anchor as trigger and response and traces a belief anchor.

column5: Every label a person carries therefore works a little like an anchor.
column7: The page says labels work like anchors, helpful or limiting; the workbook teaches the anchor idea and tests one limiting belief.

column5: A second distortion is that a belief about yourself, if it is strong enough, begins to shape what you do in ways that confirm it.
column7: The guide says a self-belief shapes behaviour so as to confirm itself; the workbook traces one such belief to its early experience and tests it.

column5: What it trains is the underlying skill of noticing your own internal state shift as it happens, so that you catch it when a tool like AI, or anyone else with a confident voice, is asking for your agreement.
column7: The page names noticing your own internal state shift as it happens; the workbook sets out the loop from event to meaning to state to behaviour and lets the reader trace one of their own.

column5: An event happens, the person gives it a meaning, and much of what they then feel comes from that meaning.
column7: The sentence gives the first steps of the loop, an event and the meaning given to it; the workbook adds the state and behaviour that follow and the outcome that returns as the next event.

column5: How you feel about what someone says depends on the meaning you give it, since the same remark can sound like an insult or a clumsy kindness.
column7: The sentence says the same remark lands differently by the meaning given; the workbook walks the reader through how that meaning sets their state and next move.

column5: Stephen Covey, in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People, separated his Circle of Control from his Circle of Concern.
column7: The sentence introduces the two circles by name; the workbook lets the reader place their own worries and choices in them with a written exercise.

column5: Epictetus drew that line two thousand years ago when he separated what is up to us from what is not, and Stephen Covey redrew it centuries later as a small circle of influence inside a larger circle of concern.
column7: The sentence describes the small inner circle inside the larger circle of concern; the workbook teaches both circles and asks where the reader's attention settles.

column5: The Circle of Concern against the Circle of Control gives daily decisions a practical filter.
column7: The sentence offers the circles as a filter for decisions; the workbook gives the reader questions and an exercise to use that filter on real worries.

column5: Below them sit the medium-term goals, of which there are usually many more, such as becoming debt-free within a set number of years, building an effective team, or keeping your skills current instead of letting them go stale.
column7: The page describes the tiers from life vision down to short-term action; the workbook sets the same pyramid in NLP and has the reader fill it in for their own life.

column5: Ideas come first, a vision second and goals last, because without a vision there is nothing for a goal to belong to.
column7: The sentence puts vision above goals; the workbook shows the four tiers from one life vision down to many short-term goals and has the reader build their own.

column5: Visionary goal setting sits inside this stage.
column7: A reader meeting goal setting inside a helping model would want the basics of how a vision breaks into long, medium and short-term goals, which the workbook teaches and applies.

column5: Positively framed goals, stated as what you are moving towards and not what you are moving away from, get their own part.
column7: The page names positively framed goals and gives one example; the workbook explains why a goal built on leaving something behind loses its pull and has the reader reframe their own.

column5: There's also a distinction between avoidance-led goals and vision-led ones.
column7: The sentence contrasts goals led by avoidance with goals led by a vision; the workbook teaches the same split as wanted and not-wanted goals and tests the reader's past resolutions.

column5: Neuro-linguistic programming (NLP) well-formed outcomes add a second layer of testing, and a goal has to be stated in the positive, as what you want and not what you want to avoid.
column7: The sentence says a goal must be stated in the positive; the workbook explains why and has the reader rewrite their own goals as places to arrive.

column5: Milton Erickson's account of what he called the critical factor sits at the centre of the idea.
column7: The page cites Erickson on the filter that turns away what is told; the workbook gives his broad, open questions as the way past that filter and lets the reader try ten of them.

column5: The Milton Model, named after the psychiatrist Milton Erickson, adds a set of language patterns to the toolkit, including chunking up and down between broad ideas and small detail.
column7: The sentence names Erickson as the source of the Milton Model's language; the workbook teaches his broad questions directly and takes one stuck problem through all ten.

column5: An open question can't be answered in one word, so the other person is free to choose where to go.
column7: The sentence defines an open question; the workbook gives the reader ten broad questions in four movements to ask without notes and a problem to practise on.

column5: Build well-formed outcomes with the transition included.
column7: The sentence tells a coach to build well-formed outcomes; the workbook gives the ladder of questions that makes an outcome well formed and has the reader apply it to one goal.

column5: Well-formed outcomes matter more than they sound as though they should.
column7: The sentence says well-formed outcomes matter; the workbook teaches the questions from what and why through to milestones and lets the reader use them.

column5: Well-formed outcomes sharpen the second half.
column7: The page lists well-formed outcomes among techniques to try; the workbook gives the outcome questions in order and a written exercise to try them.

column5: Richard Bandler proposed that people respond to problems in four ways.
column7: The sentence introduces the four responses; the workbook lays them out in full and has the reader find which one they reach for first on a real problem.

column5: Doing nothing, meanwhile, is the weakest option available at any moment of decision, since nothing changes until a choice is made.
column7: The sentence treats doing nothing as the weakest option; the workbook sets it beside solving, feeling better and tolerating, so the reader can see their own pattern across all four.

column5: The mistake a helper can make at this point is to hurry towards solving the problem as it was first described.
column7: The sentence is about solving a problem; the workbook shows solving is only one of four responses and that feeling better is not the same thing.

column5: Those three were Fritz Perls, Virginia Satir and Milton Erickson.
column7: The page names Satir among the therapists NLP's founders studied; the workbook teaches her three core beliefs and applies them to the reader's own problems.

column5: The family therapist Virginia Satir gave this pattern a proper name, the Leveller.
column7: The page uses one of Satir's ideas on how people cope; the workbook teaches her core beliefs about coping and meaning and asks the reader where coping has outweighed the problem.

column5: Virginia Satir taught that families, and marriages, run on largely unspoken rules, and that the rules come from the families each partner grew up in.
column7: The sentence introduces Satir's view of family rules; the workbook goes to her core beliefs and has the reader test what their own assumptions rest on.

column5: His Gestalt therapy focuses on present-moment awareness over analysis of the past.
column7: The page says Perls's Gestalt therapy puts present-moment awareness ahead of the past; the workbook adds where Perls's idea of owning a problem comes from and a written exercise on one problem the reader has blamed on someone else.

column5: Those three were Fritz Perls, Virginia Satir and Milton Erickson.
column7: The sentence names Perls as one of the three therapists NLP was built from; a reader curious about him gets from the workbook what Gestalt therapy is and how to work a blamed problem through as their own.

column5: In 1971 Richard Bandler and Frank Pucelik were students at Kresge College, part of the University of California Santa Cruz, and both had an interest in Gestalt therapy.
column7: The page puts Gestalt therapy at the start of NLP; the workbook explains what Gestalt therapy is and what Perls's ownership idea asks of the reader.

column5: Three words are easier to remember than six conditions, which is probably why genuineness, acceptance and empathy survived and the rest slipped from common use.
column7: The page sets out Rogers's conditions as a theory; the workbook has the reader rate one real relationship against them and choose one change.

column5: Person-centred counselling grew from the work of [Carl Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Rogers), a psychologist who set out the conditions under which people grow in books such as *On Becoming a Person*, and who named three of them: congruence, empathy and unconditional positive regard.
column7: The sentence says Rogers set out the conditions under which people grow; the workbook turns them into three attitudes the reader checks in a relationship at home or at work.

column5: Rogers is the person who founded person-centred therapy, and his approach rests on three core conditions.
column7: The page says active listening rests on Rogers's three core conditions; the workbook teaches those conditions in full and has the reader test them in one conversation.

column5: A four-stage model of interpersonal misinterpretation appears, in slightly different language, across three of the courses, which tells you something about how often it happens.
column7: The page says a four-stage model of misinterpretation runs through the courses; the workbook teaches the four stages in full and has the reader trace one misunderstanding through them.

column5: You send a message you thought was perfectly clear, and the reply comes back asking what you meant.
column7: The sentence is the gap between what was meant and what was heard; the workbook names the stages in between and shows where the meaning changed.

column5: The other person is doing the same, answering what they assume we meant, and that shows [how assumptions affect relationships](/learn/mental-wellness/quotes/how-do-assumptions-affect-relationships/) from both sides.
column7: The sentence describes the fourth stage, the listener answering an assumed meaning; the workbook lays out all four stages and an exercise to find which one went wrong.

column5: What Grossmann and Kross found is that stepping back from a problem, rather than staying immersed in it, closed the gap between how wisely people reasoned about others and about themselves.
column7: The page reports that stepping back from a problem closes the gap in how wisely people reason; the workbook gives a step-by-step way to take that step back from one past event.

column5: You're too wound up to rest, and you keep replaying something you said, or decided, or failed to do, three weeks ago.
column7: The reader of this opening knows the replay that teaches nothing; the workbook shows why replaying from inside the event fails and how to view it from outside.

column5: Next time you notice yourself replaying something you said or did, with the criticism mounting, put a pause on it.
column7: The sentence asks the reader to pause a replay; the workbook gives a way of moving outside the memory so the replay yields something to learn.

column5: The second is perceptual positions, which ask you to look at a situation from your own point of view, from the other person's and then from the side as an onlooker.
column7: The page names perceptual positions in one sentence; the workbook teaches all four, including going meta, and has the reader apply them to one situation in writing.

column5: Perceptual positions add another tool, which is to view one situation from more than one vantage point: your own, another person's, and a detached observer's watching from outside.
column7: The page offers three vantage points; the workbook adds the fourth, the view from further back, and an exercise for one situation.

column5: Most conflicts look very different from the second and third positions than they did from the first.
column7: The sentence says conflicts look different from the second and third positions; the workbook teaches those positions with the fourth and has the reader write each view.

column5: Pacing and leading form a practical pair in the section.
column7: The page names pacing and leading as a pair; the workbook teaches them with sensory acuity and the point where meeting someone turns into handling them.

column5: Matching your language to a person's channel, even slightly, makes them feel understood in a way that is hard to fake.
column7: The page says matching a person's channel makes them feel understood; the workbook teaches how to notice the channel through sensory acuity and plan a real conversation around it.

column5: That is one finding about mirroring, offered here as information and not as the reason Achology teaches immediacy.
column7: The sentence reports research on matching another person's manner; the workbook teaches pacing as the ethical form of it and draws the line against handling.

column5: A strategy is a high-level, directed plan aimed at a specific objective, and a tactic is a smaller action taken to carry out part of it.
column7: The page defines strategy against tactic in a sentence; the workbook builds on it with why a tip with no plan fades and a written exercise on one goal.

column5: Buying a planner, downloading another tracking app or signing up for a course can feel like progress, and sometimes it stands in for progress altogether.
column7: The sentence describes tools that stand in for progress; the workbook explains why single steps fade without a strategy behind them and has the reader write one.

column5: A vision on a whiteboard costs nothing, whereas a vision with a plan beneath it costs time, discomfort and a good deal of dull, repeated effort.
column7: The sentence separates a vision from a vision with a plan beneath it; the workbook has the reader write a strategy first and its tactics second for one goal.

column5: The basic move is to watch how something is done, describe it in steps and ask what could be done differently, and none of that needs another person in the room.
column7: The sentence describes the basic modelling move of watching how something is done; the workbook teaches what to ask and watch for and has the reader write questions for one person.

column5: Think of watching a skilled negotiator and writing down, step by step, what she does in the first five minutes, so that a newcomer can try the same sequence.
column7: The sentence pictures modelling as writing down what a skilled person does; the workbook teaches how to get past the tidy answer and prepare the questions.

column5: Bandura split observational learning into four processes, and if any one of them fails, the behaviour isn't copied.
column7: The page covers learning by watching others; the workbook teaches NLP's version, modelling a person who already has the result, and an exercise to prepare it.

column5: Keeping the two apart is most of what it means to reframe failure, and the rest is practice.
column7: The page separates what a failure contains from the reading put on it; the workbook sets one setback down as a breakdown and then as a breakthrough and shows why the first reading comes by default.

column5: [Her definition](https://ctl.stanford.edu/growth-mindset) of a growth mindset is the ability to reframe perceived failures as opportunities to learn and grow.
column7: The sentence defines a growth mindset as reframing perceived failures; the workbook shows how one setback reads as a breakdown or a breakthrough and how the first reading is reset.

column5: The comfort zone is where most people spend their best years, safe and familiar and rarely as satisfying as it looks from inside.
column7: The sentence calls the comfort zone safe and familiar; the workbook asks why a familiar cage can feel safer than an open door and has the reader rewrite one setback.
